title: AI Search Engines: Are They Killing the Web?
label: Trends
description: Answer engines now resolve many queries without a click. Who loses traffic, who keeps it, and what the shift means for both sides.

Table of contents

  1. From links to answers
  2. Who is losing traffic
  3. Who keeps traffic, and why
  4. The case that the web is not dying
  5. What readers gain and lose
  6. What to do about it

Answer engines now resolve many queries without a click. Who loses traffic, who keeps it, and what the shift means for both sides.

Search used to mean a list of links and a decision. Increasingly it means a paragraph written by a model, sometimes with sources attached, and often with no visit to anyone's website at all. That is no longer a prediction. It is the default behaviour of the major search products, and it arrived quietly enough that many publishers only noticed in their traffic charts.

The question people actually care about is whether this destroys the web that depends on that traffic, or merely redistributes it. The honest answer is narrower than either side of the argument usually admits, and the useful response depends on which of the two groups you are in: someone publishing, or someone reading.

From links to answers

Informational queries resolve well when synthesised. Definitions, comparisons, how-to steps and quick lookups are all cases where a reader wants a conclusion, not a ranking of candidates. Answer engines read a set of sources, compress them, and hand back a paragraph with citations. For a narrow question this is genuinely better than ten blue links, and pretending otherwise is nostalgia rather than analysis.

What changes is the click. It stops being the point of the interaction and becomes the exception, taken mostly when a reader needs the source itself: a primary document, a tool, a store, a community. Queries that are contested, expensive to get wrong, or early in a buying decision still send people through, because nobody trusts a compressed summary with a decision they have to live with.

The economics follow the behaviour. A visit that used to begin with a query and continue into a page now often ends as a read of a summary, and the reader who does click through has already been handed the conclusion. That leaves fewer visits, with more intent behind each one, which is a very different asset from the high-volume, low-intent traffic that informational listings used to deliver.

Who is losing traffic

The exposure is concentrated rather than general. Sites whose value was being an intermediary take the hit first: aggregators that restate facts available elsewhere, listicles assembled from other people's pages, and thin pages built around a question that now gets answered in place. Their function, helping a machine find an answer, is now performed by the machine itself. The second group is anyone dependent on a single channel. Loss shows up first in informational top-of-funnel visits, while branded and direct traffic holds, which is why the damage tends to be invisible in a site's own engagement numbers until it is serious.

What it means for you: if most of your visits arrive from one channel, and most of your pages restate information available elsewhere, you are exposed now rather than eventually. Rebuilding diversity is far cheaper before the decline appears in a quarterly report than after it, and it is nearly impossible once the habit of publishing for one audience has set in.

Who keeps traffic, and why

Three categories survive the shift. The first is sources carrying something the model does not already have: original data, first-hand testing, interviews, or genuinely specific experience. An answer engine that cites at all has to cite someone, and it cites the page that gave it a fact it could not generate. The second is brands people already know, because those arrive through direct entry and brand search rather than through a query that gets intercepted. The third is anything that cannot be compressed into a paragraph: a calculator, a working tool, a marketplace, a community, a product page.

What it means for you: if you publish, become the source rather than the summary. Publish the test results, the dataset, the process, the specific number nobody else has, and structure it so a machine can quote it cleanly. Our AI research workflow guide shows the reader-side version of the same habit: going to sources instead of stopping at the synthesis.

The case that the web is not dying

There is a real counter-argument, and it is worth stating properly. Answer engines still link to and cite the pages they draw from, and referral traffic from those citations behaves differently from ranked listings. Publishers negotiate licensing arrangements for content and data. Discovery has been disintermediated before, by portals, by aggregators, by social feeds, and each time the same panic was followed by redistribution rather than extinction. The strongest version of the argument is therefore not that the web dies, but that the middle gets hollowed out: generic material sitting between the top sources and the brands people already type in.

What readers gain and lose

Readers gain speed, and for low-stakes questions that is a straight win. What they lose is harder to see: the sense of who is speaking, the disagreement between sources, and the accidental discovery of a better page two links down. A confident synthesis of weak sources is still weak, and nothing in the interface signals that. This is why verification has become a reading skill rather than an editorial one. Our piece on fact-checking AI output before you publish applies to answers you read as well as text you write, and it is worth comparing formats directly in Perplexity against Google Search.

The asymmetry matters in practice. These engines are strongest on questions with settled answers and weakest exactly where the stakes rise: contested claims, recent events, anything where careful sources disagree. Knowing which kind of question you are asking is the difference between saving ten minutes and quietly inheriting somebody else's mistake.

What to do about it

If you publish, act on the traffic you can defend rather than the traffic you hope for:

  • Put something original in every substantial piece. A number you measured, a photograph you took, a question you asked. Original material is what gets cited.
  • Build a direct channel. An email list or a community survives any interface change, because nobody can intercept it.
  • Write answers people can quote. Clear definitions, short direct statements, structured headings. Machines quote clean prose.
  • Check your own analytics by intent. Separate visits to pages that inform from visits to pages that do something, and watch the first category honestly.

If you read, keep the citation habit: open the source when the decision matters, and treat the paragraph as a summary that has not been checked yet. Neither response requires believing the whole shift is good or catastrophic. It only requires accepting that the layer between question and answer has moved, and positioning yourself on whichever side of it you actually benefit from.

Frequently asked questions

Are AI search engines reducing traffic to websites?

For some sites, clearly; for others, barely. The losses concentrate on pages whose value was summarising information available elsewhere, since that is exactly what an answer engine now does. Sites carrying original data, first-hand experience, tools people use directly, or a brand people already type in keep a much larger share of their visits.

Should I stop optimising for search altogether?

No, but you should stop optimising only for search. Being useful to an answer engine and being useful to a human are increasingly the same thing: clear structure, specific claims, original evidence. The sensible response is to reduce dependence on any single channel by building direct relationships such as email lists, communities and brand recall.

Can readers trust AI-generated search answers?

As much as the sources underneath them. A synthesis of weak material stays weak, and confident phrasing hides that. Read the citations rather than the paragraph, check any figure that would change a decision, and treat an answer as a first draft of your own understanding instead of a finished one.
